opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I've been thinking about for years.

In locomotion, rewards are relatively easy to write down. You want the robot to move forward at a certain velocity, stay upright, not waste too much energy, and keep its motions smooth. Those are all quantities you can measure directly from the robot's own state, and a few terms get you surprisingly far. That's a big part of why sim-to-real reinforcement learning took off for legged robots first.

Manipulation is different in a few fundamental ways.

First, the task is usually defined in terms of the world, not the robot. If I ask a robot to fold a towel, wipe a table, or put dishes in a rack, success depends on the state of objects: deformable cloth, liquids, crumbs, articulated things. Measuring that state reliably is itself a hard perception problem. In simulation you can cheat and read the ground truth, but then you have a gap between the reward you trained on and what the robot can actually observe in the real world.

Second, manipulation tasks are long-horizon and contact-rich. The final success signal, like "the towel is folded," is very sparse. The robot almost never stumbles into it by random exploration. So people add shaping terms: get the gripper close to the corner, lift it to some height, move it over there. Every one of those terms is a human guess about *how* the task should be done, and RL is extremely good at finding loopholes. The policy will exploit any gap between what you wrote and what you meant. We've all seen robots that technically maximize the reward while doing something absurd.

Third, there's the scalability issue. Even if a skilled engineer spends a week tuning a reward for one task, that doesn't transfer to the next task. If we want general-purpose robots that can do thousands of things in homes, hand-engineering a reward for each one simply doesn't scale.

And finally, a lot of what we care about is hard to formalize at all: do it gently, do it the way a person would expect, don't knock over the cup next to it. Humans carry these implicit preferences, and they're very hard to encode as a scalar.

That's why I find the recent direction so exciting. Instead of writing rewards by hand, we can use large foundation models, vision-language models, to judge progress or success, or even have language models write reward code that we then iterate on. Combined with learning from demonstrations, which sidesteps reward design by showing the robot what to do, I think we're moving toward a regime where reward specification becomes much less of a bottleneck. But we're not fully there yet, and that remains one of the most interesting open problems in robot learning.

r001.rationale: The candidate says locomotion rewards are relatively easy to write and directly links this to sim-to-real RL taking off first for legged robots.

r002.rationale: It explains that manipulation success depends on difficult-to-measure object states and that human preferences such as gentleness are hard to formalize as a scalar.

r003.rationale: It says reward tuning for one task does not transfer to the next and that hand-engineering rewards for thousands of tasks does not scale.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one of the problems I've spent a lot of time on, because on the surface reward design sounds like it should be the easy part. You know what you want the robot to do. Just write it down. But in practice it almost never works that way, and I think there are a few reasons.

The first is that manipulation tasks are defined by outcomes, not by motions. When you say "put the cup in the dishwasher," the thing you actually care about is a final state, and that state is extremely sparse. If you only reward the robot when the cup is in the right place, it will essentially never stumble into that by random exploration. The space of arm motions and contacts is enormous. So people start adding shaping terms, distance to the cup, distance to the rack, penalties for dropping, and every one of those terms is a guess about what the intermediate progress should look like. And the robot is very good at finding the gap between what you wrote and what you meant. It will push the cup toward the rack without ever grasping it, or it will hold the cup perfectly still right above the target because that minimizes a distance term and avoids the risk of a drop penalty.

The second thing is contact. In locomotion, which is where a lot of my earlier work was, the reward is actually pretty forgiving. Forward velocity, stay upright, don't use too much torque. Those are smooth and global signals. In manipulation, everything that matters happens through contact, and contact is discontinuous. Whether the fingers are a millimeter apart or touching changes the entire dynamics. A reward that looks reasonable in simulation can produce behaviors that exploit the contact model, jittering fingers, strange wedging motions, that completely fall apart on real hardware.

And the third reason, which I think is underrated, is that we often don't actually know what we want precisely enough to write it down. Think about folding a shirt. What is the reward? There's no clean mathematical description of a well-folded shirt. Humans judge it instantly by looking, but turning that judgment into a scalar is genuinely hard. So this is why the field has moved so heavily toward demonstrations, toward learned reward models, toward using vision-language models as judges. It's not that reward design failed, it's that for a lot of these tasks the human is the only reliable source of the specification, and we're finding better ways to extract it from them.

I do think this is also one of the places where large models are changing things. If you can describe the task in language and have a model propose reward functions, or evaluate progress from images, you get a very different workflow. Early experiments there are promising, but it's still pretty fragile. The model can be confidently wrong about physical progress, and the robot will happily optimize against those mistakes.

r001.rationale: The response says locomotion rewards can be forgiving, but does not attribute reinforcement learning’s success in quadruped walking to that ease.

r002.rationale: It says a well-folded shirt has no clean mathematical description and that turning human judgment into a scalar reward is hard.

r003.rationale: It gives examples of different manipulation tasks, but does not argue that task diversity makes specifying a reward for each nearly infeasible.

astra-6.text:
I think the fundamental difficulty is that it’s often much easier to recognize a successful behavior than to describe it mathematically. If I ask a robot to pick up a cup, the goal sounds simple. But does success mean lifting it off the table? Holding it securely? Keeping it upright? And how do we express that it shouldn’t squeeze too hard or knock over something nearby?

You can give a reward only when the task succeeds, but then the robot gets very little feedback while it’s learning. Manipulation requires a sequence of precise contacts, and random exploration may almost never produce success. So we add intermediate rewards—for approaching the object, touching it, lifting it. Those help learning, but they also introduce assumptions about how the task should be done. The robot may find a way to maximize those rewards without accomplishing what we actually intended.

So there’s this tension: a simple reward can be too sparse to learn from, while a detailed reward can accidentally specify the wrong behavior. And when you change the object or the task, you often have to revisit those design choices. That makes reward design a real bottleneck for building robots that can learn many different manipulation skills.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention quadruped walking or attribute its reinforcement learning success to an easy-to-specify reward.

r002.rationale: It says successful behavior is easier to recognize than to describe mathematically and explains how that complicates defining manipulation rewards.

r003.rationale: It notes that changing objects or tasks can require revisiting reward design, but does not argue that task diversity makes specifying rewards for each task nearly infeasible.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the core difficulty is that we know what we want the robot to accomplish, but translating that intention into a numerical reward is surprisingly hard. For a simple task, you might reward the robot for moving an object close to a target. But that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it grasped the object securely, damaged it, or pushed it in a way that would fail in a slightly different situation.

And reinforcement learning is very good at optimizing exactly what you specify. If there is a shortcut in the reward, the policy may discover it. So you add another term, and then another, and you end up balancing task completion, safety, smoothness, and efficiency. Those terms can interact in unexpected ways.

In manipulation, there’s also a measurement problem. In simulation, you can often access the exact object pose or contact state. On a real robot, those quantities may be noisy or difficult to observe. A simple success reward avoids some of that engineering, but then successful behavior may be too rare for the robot to learn efficiently. So the challenge is to provide enough guidance for learning while keeping that guidance faithful to what we actually want.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reward design in manipulation but does not attribute quadruped walking success to easier reward specification.

r002.rationale: It says translating the intended manipulation outcome into a numerical reward is hard, and explains that simple measures may miss secure grasping, damage, or robustness.

r003.rationale: It does not argue that the diversity of manipulation tasks makes specifying a reward for each nearly infeasible.
